as_told.title: Sculptor Michael Richards' plane sculptures and death in the Twin Towers
as_told.place_text: Miami; World Trade Center, New York

plain: Twelve days before 9/11, an artist who had a studio in one of the Twin Towers made a work showing himself as a Tuskegee Airman, one of the Black American pilots of the Second World War, with old fighter planes flying into him. Michels tells it himself without naming a source, and calls it a painting made under an arts programme in the towers. The researcher Eric Wargo, who writes about dreams and seeing the future and cites his own book Time Loops, tells it on two episodes with more detail. He names the artist as Michael Richards and calls the work a sculpture titled Tar Baby vs. St. Sebastian. Wargo says the Lower Manhattan Cultural Council gave studios in the towers to groups of 15 artists for six months at a time. He says Richards "alone among those artists" stayed in his studio the night of September 10th and was killed there the next morning. The tellers differ on whether it was a painting or a sculpture, and they tell it because, if it is what they say, an artist pictured his own death before it happened.
